title: Everest AI POC scoping - latency & throughput SLOs
next_steps: Redwood to run initial 1k request benchmark and share raw results (Jonah)
Maya to send pricing and pilot terms
Customer to share representative request traces and sample prompts
Schedule in-person demo of Dedicated stack if baseline looks good
action_items: Jonah Reed: run baseline synthetic + replay bench, produce spreadsheet w/ TTFT & TPOT by qps and model variant (due: 2027-12-03)
Maya Patel: send pilot contract + pricing sheet and Redwood security docs (SOC2 summary, ISO) (due: 2027-12-01)
Marco Diaz: share 3 days of anonymized request traces and sample payloads (due: 2027-12-02)
Priya Nair: confirm VPC networking constraints and egress rules (due: 2027-12-04)
transcript: [00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining - Maya from Redwood here. quick roll call?
[00:08] Elena Park: Hi Maya, Elena here - CTO at Everest. we've got Marco, Priya, Samir on - thanks for setting this up.
[00:18] Maya Patel: perfect thanks. Jonah from our SE team will drive the SLO discussion - we're looking to scope the POC around latency/throughput targets and measurement plan.

[00:28] Jonah Reed: hey all. quick agenda - confirm success criteria, understand workload (qps, payload sizes, concurrency), pick TTFT vs TPOT definitions, agree p95/p99 targets, and define bench plan and timeline.

[00:42] Marco Diaz: sounds good. current stack - we run a mix of 3 LLM features: chat assistant, summarization, and a short completion API for UI autocomp. chat is the heavy one - median prompt ~120 tokens, responses ~220 tokens. avg concurrent users ~200 during peak, qps ~160.

[00:58] Priya Nair: infra note - we're on GCP right now, but we'll consider a Private deployment later. for the POC we prefer Redwood hosted but must ensure VPC peering is possible; also need KMS integration for keys.

[01:15] Jonah Reed: good. on metrics - we usually capture TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time to produce the whole output). customers often prefer TTFT for perceived latency in UI, TPOT for backend SLAs. which do you care about more?

[01:32] Elena Park: both matter. the product team wants TTFT < 250ms p95 for chat to keep UI snappy; ML team wants TPOT p95 < 800ms for average sized responses. p99 targets can be looser but we need to quantify.
[01:48] Samir Bose: to add, for autosuggest/autocomplete we need TTFT p95 < 120ms ideally, but that's a lower-latency tier - might require dedicated capacity or quantized model.
[02:03] Maya Patel: noted. quick clarification - when you say p95 < 250ms TTFT that's measured at the application edge or at the Redwood API? we should align on measurement point.
[02:16] Priya Nair: we can accept Redwood's API-side measurements as long as we see exportable traces and per-request timing logs. we need to be able to map to our traces too for end-to-end SLAs.

[02:30] Jonah Reed: makes sense. POC plan: Redwood will run server-side bench and provide logs + t-digest percentiles. we recommend a dual measurement approach - synthetic load (k6/jmeter) to stress, plus replay of your real traces to capture distribution and caching effects.

[02:47] Marco Diaz: replay is important - we have a KV cache effect where repeated prefixes hit cached KV and are much faster. cold vs warm cache will change numbers. how does Redwood account for KV cache in benchmarks?

[02:59] Jonah Reed: good call. we'll run three phases: cold-warm-hot. cold = fresh model, no cache; warm = primed cache with your trace; hot = continuous traffic to measure steady-state. we'll tag results by phase.

[03:14] Elena Park: also want to understand batch sizes - our front-end aggregates small requests; sometimes requests are batched at the gateway. benchmark should include single-request latency and batched throughput.
[03:27] Jonah Reed: we'll report per-request TTFT/TPOT for single-mode and aggregated metrics for batching - include average batch sizes, max batch size, and throughput (tokens/sec).
[03:38] Maya Patel: ok lets talk targets concretely. current baseline from your note Marco - p95 TTFT target 250ms, p99 maybe 500ms? TPOT p95 800ms, p99 1400ms? are those numbers acceptable to start?
[03:55] Marco Diaz: p99 500ms for TTFT might be aggressive but okay as a pilot target; TPOT p99 at 1.4s is fine. for autosuggest we will have a separate micro-POC with tighter TTFT targets.
[04:10] Samir Bose: timeline - we want bench data within two weeks and a short pilot for 4 weeks to validate production traffic. is that realistic?

[04:19] Jonah Reed: yes realistic. proposed timeline: Week 0 (this week) - collect traces and confirm config; Week 1 - Redwood runs synthetic + replay bench; Week 2 - share results and tune config; Weeks 3-6 - pilot with limited production traffic on hosted or dedicated reserved nodes.
[04:34] Priya Nair: reserved nodes might be needed if we can't hit p95 targets on shared capacity. what are your options for Dedicated during pilot?

[04:42] Jonah Reed: we can provision Dedicated pools for pilot; minimum commit is typically 4 GPUs for certain model sizes, but we can also do a short-term reserved trial with burst capacity. we'll include cost estimates in the pricing sheet.

[04:56] Elena Park: measurement details - we need to know where percentiles computed, error budgets, and SLA definitions. example: SLA = p95 TTFT <= 250ms measured at Redwood ingress, 99.9% uptime. also need tracing headers so we map requests.

[05:12] Jonah Reed: agreed. measurement plan bullet points: 1) define measurement point (Redwood ingress) 2) collect baseline traces from customer 3) run 3-phase bench (cold/warm/hot) 4) produce percentile tables (p50/p90/p95/p99) for TTFT and TPOT, tokens/sec, and tail latency 5) include error rate and payload success rate.
[05:31] Marco Diaz: how will you simulate concurrency and qps? our peaks are bursty - 200 concurrent users but qps spikes to 300 for short bursts.
[05:40] Jonah Reed: we'll create traffic profiles: steady-state at 160 qps, spike tests hitting 300-400 qps for 1-2 minute bursts, and ramp tests. also measure recovery time and queueing effects.

[05:52] Maya Patel: what's the instrumentation plan? we need logs, traces, and an artifact for audit. Redwood provides per-request timing and t-digest summaries; can we also get raw samples on request?

[06:02] Jonah Reed: yes - we'll provide raw sample logs for a subset (sanitized) plus the aggregated histograms. we can push data to your S3 or share a secure link. we'll also include request IDs for trace correlation.
[06:13] Priya Nair: security note - we need SOC2 summary, encryption at rest, KMS integration, and audit logs before putting any PII in traces. send over the security docs.
[06:24] Maya Patel: will do - I'll attach our SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide to the follow-up email.
[06:30] Elena Park: ok, regarding model variants - we may want to try standard 7B and a quantized 7B variant. want to measure quality vs latency tradeoff. can Redwood host both for the POC?
[06:42] Jonah Reed: yes we can host multiple variants; bench will include both. we'll report token-level cost estimates too so you can see cost/latency tradeoffs.
[06:53] Marco Diaz: on quality - we want no more than 3% regression in our eval set when switching to quantized model. we can provide eval prompts and expected outputs.
[07:03] Jonah Reed: include those evals in the bench plan - we'll run quality checks alongside latency runs and flag any regressions.
[07:12] Samir Bose: another question - how do you define TTFT precisely? is it first byte from model compute or first token emitted from Redwood to client?

[07:20] Jonah Reed: good question. we'll define TTFT as time from Redwood receiving the request to emission of the first token to the client (including routing and model compute). we'll record both server-side compute time and end-to-end emission time.
[07:33] Elena Park: for TPOT are we measuring until the last token is emitted or until the response is complete at the client? sometimes network streaming means client receives tokens over time.
[07:41] Jonah Reed: TPOT = time to produce last token at Redwood egress. for streaming, we'll provide both time-to-first and time-to-last with token counts and bytes.
[07:51] Marco Diaz: ok. what about warmup per model - does Redwood maintain KV cache across requests in hosted mode? how long to warm?

[07:59] Jonah Reed: KV cache persists per model shard and can be primed. warmup time depends on sequence length distribution - we'll estimate priming size and run a warm-phase to simulate typical session histories.
[08:11] Priya Nair: how will you simulate user sessions? session-level caching changes tail latencies.
[08:17] Jonah Reed: we'll replay traces preserving session IDs where possible so the cache semantics are realistic. for synthetic runs we'll add artificial session grouping.

[08:28] Maya Patel: let's anchor SLOs in concrete numbers in the notes: TTFT p95 <= 250ms, TTFT p99 <= 500ms; TPOT p95 <= 800ms, TPOT p99 <= 1400ms. Pilot acceptance = meet all p95 targets for warm and hot phases and no more than 1.5x degradation under 2x burst traffic. agree?
[08:51] Elena Park: yes agreed on pilot acceptance clause. also require exportable logs and the ability to correlate request IDs to our telemetry.
[08:59] Jonah Reed: noted - we'll include correlation headers and a sample logs schema.
[09:05] Marco Diaz: please also report cost per 1M tokens for each model/config so product can evaluate tradeoffs.
[09:12] Jonah Reed: will do - cost breakdown by model variant, quantization, and batching.
[09:18] Samir Bose: error budget question - if p95 misses by small amount during a one-off burst, do we fail the pilot?
[09:25] Maya Patel: we proposed grace: allow up to 5% of test windows to miss p95 by up to 10% during the pilot. failures must be reproducible and documented.
[09:37] Elena Park: good. security/compliance - send over the SOC2 and KMS docs. we may need an NDA before sharing traces with PII; we'll sanitize but legal wants a quick review.
[09:47] Maya Patel: I'll attach docs and include the legal contact. we'll also provide a sample redaction workflow for traces.

[09:55] Jonah Reed: technical bench specifics - we'll publish a spreadsheet with the following columns: test_name, model_variant, qps, concurrency, phase (cold/warm/hot), TTFT_p50/p90/p95/p99, TPOT_p50/p90/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec, error_rate, notes.
[10:12] Marco Diaz: perfect - that'll map to our internal dashboards. also include percentile histograms and raw sample traces for outliers.
[10:20] Priya Nair: network overhead - please note whether measurements include network latency to our region or are measured in a neutral region. we need region-specific numbers.
[10:29] Jonah Reed: we'll run regionally in us-central1 to match your GCP region, and we'll mark which tests include cross-region hops vs local.
[10:35] Maya Patel: any blockers on Redwood end to start bench?
[10:39] Jonah Reed: just need the traces and confirmation on model variants and target qps profile. also your contact for access to the S3 or secure upload.
[10:46] Marco Diaz: I'll drop the 3-day traces to the secure link and include sample prompts and an eval set. expect that by tomorrow EOD.
[10:53] Maya Patel: great - recap and next steps then.

[10:57] Maya Patel: recap: 1) customer to share traces and evals (Marco) 2) Redwood to run cold/warm/hot bench and deliver spreadsheet (Jonah) 3) Maya sends pricing + security docs 4) decide on Dedicated trial if needed. timeline target: bench results by 2027-12-03.
[11:15] Elena Park: sounds good. any remaining Qs?
[11:19] Samir Bose: nothing else from product for now. good call.
[11:22] Priya Nair: one last note - we'll want to run an internal load test in parallel once Redwood shares endpoints. coordinate to avoid double-hitting production pools.
[11:31] Jonah Reed: we'll coordinate windows and provide a test endpoint with throttles for pilot. thanks everyone - we'll follow up with attachments and scheduling.
[11:40] Maya Patel: thanks all - we'll send the summary and action items. bye.
[51:00] <<call ended>>
